questions.question: What is the main limitation of rule-based chatbots like ELIZA?
options: They fail immediately outside their narrow, hand-authored patterns.
They are too slow for real-time interaction.
They require a massive GPU to run.
questions.explanation: Rule-based bots use pattern matching (regex). While fast and predictable, they cannot handle any input that the author didn't explicitly anticipate.

questions.question: What is an 'LLM agent' loop as of 2026?
options: A language model that plans, calls tools, observes results, and repeats until the task is done.
A chatbot that has a very long system prompt.
A model that only responds in JSON.
A system that retrieves 100 documents for every query.
questions.explanation: Agents go beyond just chatting; they use reasoning to interact with external tools (like APIs or databases) to actually execute actions in the world.

questions.question: Why is 'hybrid routing' recommended for production chatbots?
options: It uses rules for safety-critical actions, retrieval for FAQs, and agents for open-ended queries.
It is the cheapest way to run a chatbot.
It allows the chatbot to run on both mobile and desktop.
It prevents the user from asking too many questions.
questions.explanation: Hybrid systems combine the strengths of different eras: rules provide reliability for critical tasks, while agents provide flexibility for complex queries.

questions.question: What is 'prompt injection' in the context of LLM applications?
options: When a user provides input that overrides or bypasses the system's instructions.
When a developer adds more prompts to the model.
When the model generates too much text.
When the model's training data is leaked.
questions.explanation: Prompt injection is a security vulnerability where untrusted user input trick the LLM into ignoring its original safety or task constraints.
